newsitem.title: UK: Oil supply seen matching 1998 demand surge.
newsitem.headline: Oil supply seen matching 1998 demand surge.

text.p: Robust growth in developing countries and a brighter economic outlook in the former Soviet Union will push world oil demand to record levels in 1998, but surging output should insulate consumers from higher prices, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said Friday.
World oil demand is forecast to grow by 1.85 million barrels per day (bpd) to 75.5 million bpd in 1998, slightly surpassing this year's increase of 1.75 million, the IEA said.

But producers outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) should be equal to the challenge, lifting supply by 2 million bpd to 47.2 million bpd as more than 25 fields in the North Sea come on stream and output from 1997 projects accelerates.

"The world oil market in 1998 is expected to be well supplied, as growth in non-OPEC oil production is anticipated to exceed the growth in world oil demand," the Paris-based agency said in its latest Monthly Oil Market Report.

Economists expect gross domestic product and demand growth in the former Soviet Union to be positive in 1998 for the first time this decade, more than offsetting a minor slowdown in most non-OECD regions.
"Significantly, demand in the former Soviet Union is expected to reverse course from a small decline in 1997 to modest growth," said the IEA, which monitors oil market trends for OECD members.

Surprisingly strong demand and disappointing non-OPEC performances this year and last have kept average oil prices steady at just over $20 a barrel for the last 18 months and some analysts see little reason for them to fall.

"Demand is rising at its fastest rate in 20 years ... The bias for revision to our price forecast related to fundamental items is clearly upward," said analysts at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Research in a report.

But other industry watchers said delayed production in the North Sea -- the main factor behind the IEA's recent 400,000 bpd downward revision of its 1997 non-OPEC estimate -- was stacking up and would hit the market next year, leading to lower prices or a smaller slice of the cake for OPEC.
"At some time these fields are going to come on stream. Beware, there is a lot of supply lurking around the corner," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at UBS in London.

Apart from a sharp upward revision in demand for OPEC's oil in the fourth quarter of 1997 due to its rivals' failings, the latest report from the West's energy watchdog contained few crumbs of comfort for the 11-member cartel as it prepares for the biannual ministerial meeting in Vienna later this month.
"Even after these revisions the numbers are extremely bearish. (IEA forecast) demand (in 1998) for OPEC at 25.3 million bpd is still 2 million bpd adrift of current output," said Pyne.
